title: Entangled
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: In Soto Zen practice, the goal isn't just to find inner peace or reduce stress, but to cultivate a deeper understanding of oneself and the present moment. This requires letting go of control and embracing uncertainty, allowing us to sit with our experiences without trying to change them. By doing so, we can develop a sense of fundamental okayness and connection to the world around us.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Thanks for being here.
It's almost Christmas.
Maybe three or four people asked me the last couple of days, "Do you celebrate Christmas?"
I said, "Well, you got a kid, of course we celebrate Christmas."
So anyway, Merry Christmas.
Sometimes you sit down to write a talk and you end up like more or less writing what you intend to write.
Sometimes something else happens.
This is one of the latter cases.
I wanted to share with you a little bit about a text that a group of us have been studying, and the group that's been studying together are all the people who have been shuso.
I thought half the people there aren't going to know what shuso means, so I better explain that.
And then I better explain the thing before that.
So I end up, instead of telling you very much about what we studied, I've got to spend the whole time telling you about who was there and why.
Hopefully, this will be worth listening to, and if not, we'll just record it for the records.
You can just be like a studio audience if that turns out to be the case.
A little bit about steps and stages in this school of practice.
It's funny though because the system of training, the system of meditation is, in essence, really simple, deceptively simple maybe.
We say, "Just practice.
Just sit.
Just be present.
Just introduce yourself and invite yourself into a position of stability and openness and let your life in.
Just be yourself."
Sometimes we quote Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, we call him the author of *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*.
He said, "When you are you, Zen is Zen.
Just be yourself."
Although when you hear something like that, you're like, "I don't want to be myself.
That's why I'm here, you idiot.
I'm sick of being myself.
It's painful and confusing and exhausting to be myself.
I want to be something else."
But we say, "No, just be yourself.

But be yourself more fully and more wholeheartedly with ever more curiosity, assuming nothing, with open mindedness, with Beginner's Mind, and increasing our, strengthening our willingness and our ability to feel the whole spectrum of our experience."
We kind of are often seeking a kind of narrow band, right?
We want a certain part of our experience.
Not this, not that, not this part.
So our practice is very gradually over years and decades and over lifetimes to just sit in the middle of that situation and just be ourselves and let something open organically, naturally.
We don't have much of a curriculum.
We don't have very clear steps in training.
How could we really?
How could I prescribe something for you or anybody prescribe something for anybody?
We're so different.
So our way of practice is very open, very responsive, very flexible.
That can be a little bit troublesome for us because we want a plan.
Maybe you've noticed that things seem a little like vague around here.
Our minds want order and a system, and this way of practice doesn't really provide that.
We want to know what to do next.
We want to know if we're doing it right.
We would like to feel better and know that we're making progress towards feeling better.
We want something.
We want help.
We want some help from our spiritual practice.
It might be this is by design, I hope so.
But this low structure system will help us with the underlying quality of mind that's really the problem.
The mind that wants more.
The mind that wants something different from the way things are.
The mind that is not content, no matter how much you tweak and get a better this or a better that.
This mind that's always resisting and grabbing, not settled.
It might be that our teachers created a system where it seems like there would be a plan, and once you get in the middle of it, there's no plan to help you let go of plans.
That's possible, but it's hard to really track this and rest in the middle of it.
We find ourselves trying to organize things better and having meetings and not really trusting the planlessness of it.
I have trouble tracking that too.
If I'm sitting in a little room in a teacher's seat and somebody comes with a problem, I want to help them out.
I want to help them find a plan.
What if the plan would be better to not have a plan?
We're used to a certain kind of mode, a way of being a step wise, logical way of responding where we're here, we want to be there.
Our minds are good at monitoring our progress and helping us take one more step to cross the street.
Our minds are really good at crossing streets.
Think about crossing the street actually.
How many things your mind is doing.
It has to be able to use visual information, which is actually just shapes and colors and light, and auditory information that we turn into things like cars and people and buses.
And it has to be able to operate all these muscles and step down from the curb and it has to figure out, "I'm a third of the way across, so I should keep going."
So it's very complicated, but our minds are very good at that.
Just automatic, automatic, no problem.
You can go across the street while you're also, you can somehow survive going across the street while you're reading your phone.
It's a miracle.
But when it comes to our inner journey, this kind of mind stinks.
It doesn't know how to operate.
It tries to apply crossing the street logic and gets frustrated.
Try so hard in your meditation and you seem like, "Is it working?
Am I getting anywhere?"
So it might be the system of practice is designed to help us feel into another kind of mind, a different kind of mind than the one that's good at crossing the street.
Dropping through and below and around and in between that busy mind that is so involved with inadequacy and lack.
Maybe we have to abandon having a plan and needing a plan in a profound and important way.
And we need a lot of support for that.
We need some structure to be able to do that.
Sometimes we can feel in a deep way in our gut that actually we're okay, feel into the fundamental kind of okayness of things just the way they are.
So our way involves simple things.
We don't have to get too complicated or subtle or existential about this.
It's wonderful just to be in a quiet room for an evening.
What a rare thing, this busy world, to spend a quiet evening just breathing with friends.
To relax a little bit.
To shed a little tension.
Straighten up the body a little bit.
Kind of feel as you sit things opening again sometimes.
That's what it feels like to sit up, and there's nothing wrong with that.
That's a perfectly great way to practice.
Just to have a little release, a little stress reduction.
But I think our way of practice is much deeper than stress reduction.
A radical feeling into our patterns and our stuckness and radically not seeking solutions.
Just being in the middle of what is.
It's a little tricky in a way.
You would think Zen would just help you like cut through all that stuff and get to peace.
To get rid of craziness or anger or addiction or confusion.
Sometimes in Zen there's language that sounds that way—cutting through, getting to the other side, awakening.
Maybe it does actually work that way.
Maybe we can cut through some of the layers, peel some of the onion, drop out of some of the habitual patterns that are just causing us suffering and difficulty.
We can once in a while notice a thought arising and act on it.
Just see it's just a thought.
I don't have to do that.
And there is a kind of freedom involved in getting rid of some of this stuff, a kind of freedom that reinforces our peacefulness in a way.
But also a kind of freedom that if we are not careful just reinforces a deeply held view that we're not free, that there's something to do and there's nothing to do.
I wish all this was simpler.
I really do.
But I think it's better for us that it's not.
So there actually are a few steps of training.
I'm kind of gradually getting towards this thing about the shuso that we're studying.
I figure it would be good to have the roadmap to the non-road.
So here's some steps in training.
First step: just show up.
That's the first step.
You might become a member of the Sangha.
We appreciate that.
We've got to pay the rent to become somewhat regular and engaged in meditation practice.
To come to the Zendo once in a while.
To try practicing at home.
To read a little bit.
Just to get curious about practice and start engaging with it.
Dabbling with it.
Experimentation with it.
Having conversations with more experienced practitioners or with a teacher or teachers.
Hanging out in the lobby here, having conversations, just being around.
So maybe that's step one, stage one.
And this is not a big deal.
Maybe we'd have more members if we made a big deal about this.
But we don't make a big deal about this.
We never say, "Tonight we want to congratulate George for entering stage one."
We could, but we don't.
We just appreciate the presence of one more seeker, one more confused, beautiful human being to hang around with.
What a miracle.
Another member of the family is here, whether they quite realize they're in a family or not.
This can include just quietly practicing without talking to anybody.
We want to honor that as a way to be in the first stage.
When I was first practicing in Santa Cruz after Kenando, that's the way I practiced.
I didn't want to talk to anybody.
I just wanted to sit and leave.
Once in a while they invite me to stay for tea, and I would find some excuse to get out of there as fast as possible.
I did.
And this first step is plenty.
This is enough.
Just to be in the stream, just to touch some sense of presence, stability, resting in the middle of our life, whether we understand it or it seems to be a good idea or a bad idea.

And one of the qualities I think maybe of the stage one practice, which probably is true of all of them, but it's especially true in stage one, is just if you ask the stage one person, "Well, why are you doing this?"
They won't really have a very good answer.
Like, "Oh, I don't know.
Isn't that a good idea?
I don't know.
Well, what is this anyway?"
So that's plenty.
One of the qualities of Soto Zen, my favorite quality I think of Soto Zen, is any one practice is complete.
Is enough.
Is sufficient.
Stage one is all the stages.
No need to go on.
But we can't help it.
Our conditioned mind tells us, if he just told us about stage one, stage two has got to be better, right?
It doesn't have to be that way.
It's just the way we think.
So maybe we can do these additional stages or steps if you choose to.
With also some curiosity about that assumption that we're going somewhere.

So the second stage or step of practice might be to start stepping into the roles in the Zendo, in the organization, to ring the bells, to learn how to orient the new one stage one people to come along, to start coming to meetings and having opinions on the email, doing the shopping, cleaning the building, noticing a little more what's going on and getting more involved.
And this is a great part of Zen training.
And what's great about this stage is we learn very experientially that it's not just meditation, that it's a whole body and mind practice and that it also involves the others.
It involves rubbing up against each other in various ways.
Sometimes they use the analogy of dirty potatoes in a tub, a tub full of water.

Like a great way to at least, you don't get them all clean, but a great way to get potatoes pretty clean, you know, if you have a whole lot of potatoes from the field, is you put them in a big tub full of water and just stir them around, and it's because they're rubbing into each other that they're getting clean, or a gem polisher.

And so lately we've been thinking a lot about that aspect of rubbing up against each other and trying to come up with guidelines and teachings and agreements about how we'll actually work with that in a constructive way when that rubbing is not like a sweet little, you know, but like, "Why did she say that to me?"
And this can be an incredibly powerful practice because we start to care a lot.
We care sometimes very passionately, sometimes very quickly.
That really impresses me sometimes.
I've been here for, you know, a little while, you know, I was like very intense about doing it the right way.
And the great advantage of caring a lot about doing it just the right way is then it's ineffably beautiful when it's just right and incredibly painful when it's not.

The bells are rung in the wrong order, the organizational structure is overly vertical or overly horizontal, or the committee is not properly formulated, or the consultation wasn't done, or you name it.
Then we really have something to work with.
And we suffer and we hope to learn.
And what are we learning about?
Well, sometimes we think we're learning how to ring the bells or learning how to create a harmonious organizational structure.
But really, we're learning about our own mind and our own heart.
One of the qualities of stage two practice is we become very vulnerable, and depending on our karma, that vulnerability can express itself in different ways.
We might become very sensitive, easily hurt by a stray gesture, a tone of voice, or a poorly chosen word, or we become prickly and aggressive.
And this doesn't sound too like Zen.
We have the disadvantage of Zen being like an adjective in our culture, but really, that's Zen.
Really, that's training.

And the reason why it's training and not just like organizational optimization and ritual, like professional ritual certification, is because meditation supports us in being curious about where all this is coming from.
We start to notice some gaps and some fuzziness and some mistakes in our assumptions about ourselves and the world.
We start to realize it's a little more complicated than that, and that it might be what so-and-so said to me, and it might be some deeper factors in my heart that are being activated.
And it takes a lot of commitment because we're engaging with our suffering and we're buoyed up by our joy.
We commit and we recommit to radically taking responsibility for our own patterns and our own clinging.
And we're tremendously supported by the fact that we know, on a good day, everyone else is doing the same.
That's the other thing that turns some of the things that get a little wonky into training and safety, because we know we have this shared aspiration to wake up.
If something does something we find difficult, we start with inquiry into our own mind in the process of working with that situation.
We soften ourselves with our aspiration to be kind, to be open, to be patient, to be generous.
We're inspired by the ancestors and the Buddhas.
We're inspired by the teachings and we do our best.
And this complicated ritual lies practice.
Whether it's a religion or not, I don't know.
I'm just having an interesting debate about that.
Is this a religion?
I don't know, but it's definitely a good laboratory.
We like science, right?
So we can say it's a laboratory.
It's just words, right?
Is it religion or science?
I don't know, but a laboratory to practice with our hearts.

I like to joke that the great thing about Zen, and this is really true in stage two, the great thing about Zen in spiritual practice, is that we care so passionately about all the details and that the details do not matter at all.
Just like the first stage of practice, this second stage of practice is complete and thorough.
You don't have to do anything else.
But then there's the third stage.

The third stage of practice might be going through the process of receiving the precepts and doing a special ceremony, a public sangha ceremony, which involves private and cooperative preparation over months, sometimes longer.
We call the ceremony jukai, which is just Sino-Japanese for receive precepts.
This is an empowerment ceremony, a commitment ceremony.
It involves the process of study and of sewing a special garment by hand.
I have little itty bitty pieces of fabric.
This is a powerful ceremony, not done casually because of its power.
You have to prepare for months.
You have to study these ethical guidelines, the precepts, but not just memorize them, but study them in an honest and humble and sincere way in the context of your own life.
Sometimes we reveal stuff about us that we're not too fond of, and we grow through that.
And the study of the precepts is such a powerful way to integrate.
So in this stage it might be we integrate more with the rest of our life off the cushion, outside the zendo, using these precepts as little magnifying glasses.
Suddenly I have to have reading glasses, so I'm relating to this analogy of little magnifying glasses.
We have a kind of habitual narrative view every moment of our life: this is me going along doing my things, this is how it's going.
I have an opinion about how it's going, so if somebody asks me, I can say, "Oh, I'm having such-and-so day."
We all know that's a little bit limited.

But the precepts, especially as it is empowered and supported by this ceremony on the horizon, supports a pause, pressing the pause button in our narrative making, so that we can see our life in a different light, from a different angle, by taking up a precept as the focus, as the lens.
One of them, for instance, is, "A disciple of Buddha maintains modesty, does not praise self at the expense of others."
A disciple of Buddha maintains modesty, does not praise self at the expense of others.
So you learn a lot if you're bringing that up, like, "Oh, how am I thinking about myself and talking about myself and thinking about others to them and with other people."
We learn so much about comparison, about judgment, about holding ourselves up or holding ourselves down.
And actually, the sort of traditional teaching on that particular precept is, "Don't hold yourself above others, don't hold yourself below others, don't hold yourself as the same as others."
So that's interesting.
What really makes you curious.
And in a practical way, working with that kind of precept is a fabulous way to study judgmental thoughts.
For a while, that was like my primary meditation object.
I don't know how many thousand judgmental thoughts there were per hour.
Judgment, judgment, judgment, judgment.
Maybe now it's only a hundred.
So in the third stage, if we are in the right situation, it's appropriate and helpful to take up this practice of precepts empowered by this ceremony, we can really soften.
We can really merge with the universe through this practice.
And actually, noticing your conduct and mind more fully, while you also have some responsibility to report back to your teacher or your Dharma colleagues, it's very powerful.
And it's a sort of first in this system.
It's sort of the first real engagement with the student-teacher archetype, which is a central archetype in Zen Buddhism.
In the third stage, the teacher comes more into play.
And the teacher is such a powerful trope, a powerful idea.
We tried to explore some aspects of the student and the teacher in the talks we had at Rohatsu.
You weren't there, or you were there, but you slept through them.
You might want to listen.
I think they were interesting.
Jeff and I both spoke about this.
We kind of picked one line on it.
There are many, many aspects, so we picked one aspect of it.
It's a very rich thing, very useful, very potentially troublesome.
And in the Zen tradition, it's seen as very essential.
There are various lists of what are the essentials of Zen, and the teacher is always on the list.
Confusing and easily misunderstood, potentially incredibly helpful, potentially dangerous.
There are so many stories of abuse through the teacher-student situation, and yet it's central to our tradition.
So it's really kind of like one of our Dharma questions is, "21st century sensitive people and feminists, how do we work with that?
How do we hold it in a way that's skillful?"
Because we can't really throw it away.
So in our system, you don't exactly become the teacher's student in this stage, though, the stage of receiving the precepts of Chukai.
It's a little softer and more relative.
The way I think about it is the relationship warms up, warms up a little or a lot between the student and the teacher receiving the precepts, whom they're receiving the precepts from.
If you feel like it after Chukai, you can hang around and say, "So-and-so is my teacher, Norman's my teacher, Tim's my teacher, or whoever he is."
If you want to, that's fine.
If you have a license or a little card, nobody writes it down anywhere.
There is a special ancestor paper you get where you're on the list.
So in that way, you are, I guess, in the lineage and the teacher's student.
But we hold it pretty softly, with Chukai as a kind of a marker, a kind of a warming of the relationship.
And it's interesting, some of the other lineages and some very close lineages to us have a totally different attitude about that.
The lineages coming from Minnesota, like Jeff in Seattle, they don't feel that Chukai has a wit to do with student-teacher relationship.
You need a preceptor, you need to be practicing, it's about commitment to the precepts.
They have a different thing for student and teacher.
In others, it's like a very strong student-teacher thing.
If you receive the Chukai from somebody, you are their student, and you need to have a certain relationship with them.
The Salt Spring Island group, I think, makes sense with Peter Levitt.
But we have a kind of middle way idea, I guess.
So if you want to try to define stages of practice, maybe Chukai is the third stage, and that's enough.
Goodness gracious.
Our way isn't to attain anything, really.
Suzuki Roshi also said, "Our way is the way of no gaining idea."
No gaining idea.
And yet he bequeathed this whole system on us, too.
But really, it's true to come back again and again and again to the central trope that our way is the way of continuous practice.
Just sitting, just showing up for your life, just paying attention.
When you walk, see if you can actually just walk.
This is really a radical thing to do.
If we pay attention, we realize we're doing anything but.
When you sit, just sit.
When you eat, just eat.
These are kind of standard Zen phrases.
They don't sound like much, but this is really a revolutionary way to live, turning around and returning to the root of just being a human being.
I forgot to warn you, this is kind of a long talk, too, and as it fits to continue our practice in a steady way, with the Sangha, with the Zendo, somewhere in the center of your life.
But there's room for lots more.
The outward form of our practice can take all kinds of shapes.
It'd be way too simplistic to think if we don't see somebody at the Zendo for a while, maybe even a long while.
It'd be simplistic and foolish to think, "Oh, she stopped practicing, he stopped practicing," or something like that.
We really don't know.
Everything is practice.
Life is practice.
And sometimes, right after Jukai, actually something shifts, something happens, you know, going through kind of a powerful ceremony like that.
And you don't always just kind of cruise through, you know, acting the same way you did before.
Sometimes you don't see somebody for a while after that.
And that's okay.
I admit, I always hope that the person's karma and their intention and their circumstances will bring them right back to the Zendo to warm their hearts and share that warmth with us from a seat here.
But it doesn't always work that way.
And we need to include the full range of expression of our practice.
And Jukai, this receiving the precepts, doesn't imply a lifetime commitment at all.
I usually say you wouldn't want to do that unless you're pretty sure you wanted to continue formal practice for maybe three years, five years, something like that.
But after that, you know, it's a rich life.
There's so many ways to practice and be and engage.
Maybe after a while, it's time to just put the rakusu, the special garment, on the shelf and express your practice life in some other way.
We don't want to make the Zendo a prison with a life sentence.
So the fourth and fifth and sixth steps, I'll try to be a little briefer for here.
I'm getting finally where I want it to end up.
It can happen in some different orders.
So here's a typical order, probably.
The fourth step might be to be shuso.
Shuso, that word actually means head seat.
Head seat, like this kind of seat.
This is another empowerment and a taking on of responsibility.
But here the responsibility is a leadership job to lead the sangha for the course of an intensive period of practice.
A practice period.
We have one coming up in January.

The stuff the shuso does, the outward stuff that you can see, includes teaching a class, a class on dharma, giving their first formal dharma talks with all the people in the circumstance, sitting literally in the teacher's seat to give a talk.
They meet individually with sangha members over a cup of tea and in the end of the period they perform a special question and answer ceremony.
Big deal public ceremony.
And that's the stuff that actually something inner is happening that's much more important.
All of this supports the possibility of the shuso, the person in this role, being in a deeply supportive and mutualistic relationship with the whole sangha.
A mysterious interconnection that emerges, that arises because everyone in the sangha comes forward to support and empower the shuso and to help her hold that role.
And the shuso's willingness to step into that seat, to sit down there, to sit in that seat, enables that to emerge and happen.
So the shuso is like the spark or the seed.
But they can't do it on their own.
One never feels ready to do this.
Never.
I had somebody who felt super ready and I said, "No, that means you're not ready."
But if you think you're not ready, you might be ready.
And people told me the opposite.
"It would never be shuso.
It would be impossible for me to do that."
And that is actually true.
You can't do it.
It's a powerful training in letting go of your individual self as like the agency.
We think we are kind of self-powered, but we know we are not.
We know we are really powered by the whole universe and by relationship and interconnection.
The shuso training is a very direct way to find that out for yourself; you have to show up.
You have to do the outer stuff that you are supposed to do.
But when you show up, you are not doing it; you are in Buddha's seat in a radical way that in that context you cannot escape from.
This can be difficult and challenging, and really beautiful.
Somehow it always works out well; I do not know how.
It always works out well.
Each person expresses their own way, their particular quirks and personality are still present, and yet something shines through each person so beautifully.
This is particularly obvious in the final ceremony.
In the final ceremony, you sit up here, and like twenty, thirty, or forty people in the middle of a very formal and slow ritual ask you very deep, personal, and profound questions.
You do not have time to think about it, and you are supposed to respond; you are supposed to answer.
You do not have any time to think about it, and in fact, you might not even know the person.
You just respond.
So obviously, you cannot be responding from the usual way of figuring something out to say; you just respond, or more accurately, a response appears seemingly coming out of your mouth.
Most people who do that ritual who sit in the shuso seat cannot remember a lot of what they said, and that is why it is a little debatable whether they actually said it.
In our system of training, being shuso is also a teaching empowerment since they were in a teacher role.
So it empowers them towards being a teacher.
After being shuso, if your shuso teacher and the local teacher, if they are different, agree, it is a good idea you start doing teacherly things to some extent.
You can offer formal dharma talks, and you can start doing formal interviews during zazen.
You are essentially like a teacher teaching under supervision.
When these stage four people, stage four teachers, former shūsōs do the interviews, we give it a little different name, a little different format.
We can talk about that another time.
We are actually investing some resources now and soon to make that more possible here.
So soon we will have much better availability to do private interviews; we call them practice discussion with the people who have done this shuso training.
It is totally possible now; we have to ask them and arrange it.
We are not very consistent with informing you that that is an option, but we are going to work on that.
When we started our mentorship program, which is a wonderful new program, not everyone is able to be involved in it.
The first pilot of it was small; we invited everyone who had done this who had done shuso to be the mentors.
That has been wonderful, and we are going to do another round of that soon.
From there, there is a lot of other stuff which I will abstain from talking about.
You might, that is again plenty, enough, no reason to go further.
But from there, you might become a priest.
You might also do a newly more recently invented stage called lay entrustment.
Once you become a priest, there is a long period of additional training.
We often say that when you ordain as a priest, you are ordaining as a novice priest, and like you are a baby, a baby priest.
So there is an additional ordination called, somewhat confusingly, dharma transmission full ordination, and then you can become an abbot in various other stuff.
These are all these stages of practice.
Lately, now we have so many people, five or six, who have been shuso and can be empowered to teach.
I have been trying to, we have been trying to get together and train and practice together and study together.
So this was a very long preamble to tell you about our study meeting.
I want to share with you a little bit about that.
I figure maybe a little context is good.
Once in a while we should say all this stuff.
We have been studying a text by Dogen, who is seen as the founder, a twelfth-century Japanese priest seen as the founder of Soto Zen.
Interestingly enough, this text is about stages of practice, and about freedom.
The text is called Twining Binds.
So imagine binds wrapped all around you, twining binds.
We kind of feel that way, right?
Reality kind of has this little tangled, or maybe our mind has this tangled, or maybe we think it is a whatever personality has this tangled.
In the central part of this essay by Dogen, and Dogen is a little hard to read, so that is why we are really like teaming up on Mr.
Dogen trying to read him.
He tells a famous Zen story.
This is a story of Bodhidharma, who is the legendary first ancestor of Zen in China.
Probably was a real person, but nobody is really sure, but a person on whom many legends have been attached.
After many years of training, he had a small sangha.
Why do I feel bad that we do not have that many people?
He had four students; that was the whole sangha, four students.
The most important and powerful teacher in the history of Zen had four students, so that is good to notice.
At the end of the training, he kind of like asked them, they had a graduation kind of like asked them, "What have you learned from all your training?"
And his four students, one at a time, told him something about their understanding, and he responded.
Here is the story.
Bodhidharma once said to his students, "The time has come.
Can you express your understanding?"
One of the students, Daofu, said, "My present view is that we should neither be attached to letters nor apart from letters and allow the way to function freely."
Daofu said, "My present view is we should neither be attached to letters nor apart from letters and allow the way to function freely."
Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my skin."
This is praise.
"You have attained my skin."
Then the nun Song Shi said, "My view is it is like the joy of seeing Akshoba Buddha, Akshoba's Buddha."
That is what I said.
